item.title: [Critical] Citrix has now patched three exploited NetScaler zero-days since 27 September — the first two were in use for weeks before disclosure, and upgrading alone does not remove an intruder already inside the gateway
item.category: Top Story
item.description: Citrix published security bulletin CTX697096 on 27 September, fixing eight flaws in NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway, CVE-2026-88771 through CVE-2026-88778, and confirmed that two of them were being exploited. CVE-2026-88771 is improper input validation that lets an unauthenticated attacker execute commands, and it affects every deployment, including the default configuration. CVE-2026-88772 is a memory overflow that can lead to code execution or denial of service where DTLS is enabled, which it is by default on VPN virtual servers. Citrix rates both CVSS v4 9.5; the fixed builds are 14.1-73.37 and 13.1-64.23 or later, with FIPS builds listed separately. The bulletin came a day after watchTowr warned that two NetScaler flaws were being exploited before any fix existed. CISA added both to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day with a 30 September deadline, now passed, saying threat actors “are actively exploiting these vulnerabilities globally”, and advised preserving forensic evidence before patching. The Dutch NCSC reported exploitation at multiple Citrix customers worldwide. The activity is older than the disclosure: Mandiant and Google’s threat intelligence group trace it to early September, and Unit 42 to 21 August. Victim counts depend on who is counting. Mandiant says dozens of organisations in government, education, technology, financial services, telecoms and legal and professional services across North America and Europe; Arctic Wolf counts at least 78; researcher Kevin Beaumont, by his own tracking, counted more than 100 by 29 September. Mass, opportunistic exploitation followed watchTowr’s root-cause write-up on 28 September. LevelBlue and Google describe what intruders leave behind: a PHP web shell called WHIPSHOT, a Python tunneller called SLAPSHOT, a rogue superuser account named sec_monitor, the appliance configuration archived from /flash/nsconfig and taken, and poisoned logs. Mandiant describes the actors as advanced and suspected state-sponsored; no group has been named. Its warning is the operational point: “Upgrading alone will not eradicate post-exploitation access or address stolen credentials.” A third flaw followed. Citrix disclosed and fixed CVE-2026-88779 in bulletin CTX697174, a memory overflow that affects only appliances configured as a SAML service provider or identity provider (CVSS v4 8.7; fixed in 14.1-73.41 and 13.1-64.28 or later). Citrix says it has seen targeted attacks that can cause denial of service and has identified no impact on the integrity of customer data. CISA added it to KEV on 4 October with a 7 October deadline. watchTowr reproduced it as a crash-only bug and suspects it is being used to knock appliances over to speed up exploitation of CVE-2026-88771. One researcher reported signs of code execution; watchTowr and Citrix describe a crash. In the Netherlands, the Ministry of the Interior took its Citrix environments offline and patients at two hospitals could not view their records; those were precautionary shutdowns, not confirmed compromises. No airport, airline or air navigation service provider has been named. Our assessment of why it leads this page: NetScaler Gateway is a common front door for airline crew and operations portals, engineering and MRO applications and integrator access into terminal systems, so a gateway compromised before it was patched is a possible path toward the OT DMZ, not only a data problem. These flaws are distinct from CVE-2026-19490, the authentication bypass added to KEV on 9 September (see the CVE-2026-19490 card). - Citrix bulletins CTX697096 and CTX697174; CISA alert and KEV catalog; Dutch NCSC, Mandiant, Google, Unit 42, Arctic Wolf, LevelBlue and Kevin Beaumont as reported by Cybersecurity Dive, SecurityWeek, The Hacker News and Help Net Security; watchTowr assessment via SecurityWeek - CVE-2026-88771 and -88772 patched and added to KEV 27 Sep 2026 (due 30 Sep, passed); CVE-2026-88779 added to KEV 4 Oct 2026, due 7 Oct 2026; watchTowr crash-only assessment reported 5 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] A China-linked crew is emptying self-hosted code repositories of SCADA and HMI source — and aerospace is on the victim list
item.category: Incident — State-linked source-code and credential theft from self-hosted developer infrastructure
item.description: Acronis threat intelligence, published on 13 September and reported on 14–15 September, describes a campaign it attributes with moderate confidence to a China-linked actor it calls Red Heron, exploiting a critical remote code execution flaw in the self-hosted Gitea code platform, CVE-2026-60004, since 29 July. The actor scanned 1,386 internet-facing Gitea instances across seven countries and compromised 11 organisations in five countries, by Acronis’s count (some secondary reports give higher figures) — the victim set spanning aerospace, telecommunications, government, elections and defence alongside industry. Two victims define the objective: a Taiwanese industrial-automation company whose stolen repositories covered SCADA and HMI tooling, IoT platform integrations and network-sniffer products, and a Canadian renewable-energy firm from which infrastructure maps, configuration secrets, SSH host keys and internal tokens were taken. The implant, a custom loader Acronis calls JITTERLY with an embedded Linux rootkit named SIXZUT, supports more than thirty post-exploitation commands. Nothing here is aviation-specific and no airport or airline has been named, but the pattern is the one that reaches this sector indirectly: MRO software houses, baggage and BMS integrators and ground-systems developers routinely keep deployment configurations, VPN profiles, device credentials and site diagrams in self-hosted repositories that sit outside anyone’s OT security programme. Stolen host keys and infrastructure maps are not the attack; they are the preparation for one that arrives later looking like legitimate maintenance access. GreyNoise research published on 21 September says the Chinese-speaking actor behind the Zyxel GS1900 switch campaign is related to, or the same as, the one behind earlier WordPress and Gitea exploitation. GreyNoise itself assesses that actor as “the same or related to” Red Heron, citing a shared command-and-control domain, malware family and the July Gitea exploitation; that is GreyNoise’s assessment, not a confirmed attribution. No new development in the Acronis research has been reported as of 27 September. - Industrial Cyber and The Hacker News reporting on Acronis threat-intelligence research into the Red Heron campaign - Exploitation traced to 29 Jul 2026; campaign reporting published 14–15 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Berlin Brandenburg stops all flying for 45 minutes on a drone sighting, its 28th drone this year against eight in all of 2025 — the gap is detection, not defence
item.category: Incident — Airspace intrusion and detection; no cyber component
item.description: On the evening of Wednesday 23 September, Germany’s air navigation service DFS closed Berlin Brandenburg’s northern runway after a drone was sighted at about 20:00 local time. It closed the southern runway at 20:20 and lifted the closure at 21:05, dpa reports, leaving the airport with no take-offs or landings for about 45 minutes. Numerous flights were delayed and several were diverted. The Federal Police searched and found nothing, and Brandenburg police have opened an investigation into dangerous interference with air traffic. No operator or motive has been identified. Some early English-language reports gave the closure as about five minutes, apparently misreading the time zone; dpa’s timeline gives 45. The trend matters more than the single event. DFS figures reported by dpa put drones recorded at BER at 28 in the first half of 2026, against eight in the whole of 2025, and flying was suspended seven times in the half-year. Earlier in the month, Brussels Airport halted traffic for roughly half an hour on the evening of Friday 12 September after a drone was sighted near the airfield; no injuries or damage were reported and movements resumed once the area was cleared, with the drone’s origin and intent unattributed. The following day Vilnius closed for 38 minutes on a drone alert that scrambled a NATO jet before the object was confirmed to be a flock of birds. Both follow the US Labor Day weekend incursion at San Diego that grounded around 400 flights, where the TSA reportedly could not identify the operator and coverage noted that US airports carry no mandatory drone-detection requirement at all. None of this is a cyberattack and none of it should be filed as one. It belongs on this page because the operational consequence is identical to an OT failure and lands on the same people: a ground stop cascades into stand and gate reallocation, jet-bridge and ramp re-sequencing, baggage re-flow and fuel and de-icing re-planning, and the decision to stop or resume is increasingly taken from software — counter-UAS detection feeds, ground-movement displays, airfield lighting control — that few airports treat as operational technology with an integrity requirement. Vilnius is the instructive one: the cost was not the drone, it was the ambiguity. - dpa reporting on the Berlin Brandenburg closure and DFS drone statistics, via Der Tagesspiegel; Reuters reporting on the Brussels Airport halt, with IJR on the Vilnius closure and NATO scramble and Tech Times on the San Diego grounding and the absence of a US detection mandate - Berlin Brandenburg 23 Sep 2026; Brussels 12 Sep 2026; Vilnius 13 Sep 2026; San Diego over the Labor Day weekend, 4–7 Sep 2026, carried as preceding context

item.title: [Not Cyber] UK air traffic failure traced to a software defect in aircraft code allocation — NATS’ preliminary report describes a timing fault, not an attack
item.category: Context — ATC operational failure; preliminary report finds a software defect, and cyber was ruled out by the operator
item.description: This is not a cyber incident. It is carried here, clearly labelled, because it is the aviation infrastructure story of the period and readers will reasonably have wondered. On 8 September a failure at NATS, the UK air navigation service provider, forced Heathrow to suspend arrivals and disrupted Gatwick and Manchester, affecting more than 2,000 flights across 8–9 September. NATS’ preliminary report, published on 18 September, places the cause in a small part of the National Airspace System: a software defect in the code that allocates aircraft identification codes. A code request was paused when a higher-priority task pre-empted it, and the update did not complete; Reuters quotes the report as saying that had the higher-priority request arrived “even one millisecond earlier or later, the update would have completed normally.” Restrictions lasted about six hours and clearing the backlog took more than two days. NATS says a mitigation is in place while a permanent fix is safety-tested and deployed. Chief executive Martin Rolfe, who had already ruled out cyber on 10 September, dismissed speculation of military interference and said the fault is unrelated to the 2023 outage; the early accounts blaming an anomalous military flight plan are not supported by the stated cause. Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander called the failure “completely unacceptable” and has tasked the Civil Aviation Authority with an independent review of NATS’ findings, its resilience investment plans and regulatory accountability. A full report is to follow, and NATS proposes a further £1bn of investment by 2033. For aviation OT teams the lesson is availability engineering rather than attack defence: a defect that only surfaces when two tasks collide within a millisecond is exactly the kind of fault conventional testing can miss, so the useful questions are how your own flight-critical systems behave when an update stalls and how quickly you recover when one does. Addendum, 21 September: FlightGlobal reports that a separate “connectivity” issue at NATS’ Prestwick centre in Scotland caused delays at several airports less than two weeks after the 8 September failure. No cause has been published, NATS has not linked it to the earlier defect, and nothing in the reporting suggests a cyber element. We carry it as an unattributed operational fault and will update if NATS publishes a cause. - NATS preliminary report of 18 Sep 2026, with Reuters reporting on its findings and the Transport Secretary’s response; earlier AeroTime and AP reporting on the disruption and Martin Rolfe’s BBC Radio remarks ruling out cyber - Failure 8 Sep 2026; cyber publicly ruled out 10 Sep 2026; preliminary report published 18 Sep 2026; Prestwick connectivity disruption reported 21 Sep 2026, cause not published

item.title: [High] GAO: the FAA cannot see spectrum attacks on aircraft communications in real time, and the ACARS and CPDLC datalinks could carry a forged clearance
item.category: Research — GAO audit of aircraft datalinks and spectrum-threat monitoring; no exploitation reported
item.description: The US Government Accountability Office published GAO-26-108439 on 21 September, titled “Aviation Cybersecurity: Enhanced Air Safety Requires FAA to Better Mitigate Threats to Aircraft Communications.” Auditors examined the text-based datalinks that carry messages between aircraft, airline operations and air traffic control — ACARS and Controller-Pilot Data Link Communications — and found weaknesses in authentication, encryption and protocol design such that, in GAO’s words, “a malicious actor could transmit fraudulent clearance cancellations, possibly leading to flight delays or safety issues.” On the spectrum side, GAO found that the FAA acknowledges jamming and spoofing as threats but “did not have a defined, real-time monitoring and detection capability for all spectrum-related threats,” and that its risk assessments and security documentation for the National Airspace System are incomplete. GAO makes nine recommendations, covering NAS risk assessments, real-time spectrum-threat monitoring, interagency coordination and stronger authentication and encryption for aircraft communications; the Department of Transportation concurred with all nine, and all nine were open at publication. This is an audit, not an incident. GAO reports no exploitation of either weakness; the report is carried because it is the most substantive primary-source aviation item of the fortnight, not because anything happened. It matters to this page for two reasons. The datalink finding belongs to airlines and their communications providers, and it puts on the record that a message channel crews act on is not authenticated. The spectrum finding is the same problem the Jammertest work exposed for GNSS, stated at national scale: a signal that is manipulated rather than removed produces no alarm anywhere in the chain, and nobody currently owns detecting it. - US Government Accountability Office report GAO-26-108439, read from GAO’s product page; AeroTime coverage of 22 Sep 2026 for context - Report published 21 Sep 2026; nine recommendations open, DOT concurred

item.title: [High] Norway spent forty minutes convincing a rescue helicopter it was somewhere else — and the avionics never reported a fault
item.category: Research — GNSS spoofing against airborne receivers; controlled exercise, not an attack
item.description: At Jammertest 2026, the annual open interference exercise on Andøya, researchers escalated a spoofing signal on 10 September until a rescue helicopter’s GPS display showed a false position out over the Norwegian Sea and a track of tight overlapping turns, while the aircraft in fact flew normally. The finding worth carrying is the detection asymmetry rather than the spectacle: jamming announces itself as signal loss and crews are trained for it, whereas spoofing leaves the receiver confidently reporting data that is internally consistent, plausible and wrong. This was a controlled test, not an in-the-wild incident, and no aircraft was endangered. It lands against a real backdrop the researchers cited — RAF aircraft encountering GPS jamming near the Russian border and daily GNSS interference over Sweden through 2026 — and it reinforces the updated jamming and spoofing guidance EASA issued to operators in July 2026. For airport operators the read-across runs past the flight deck. GNSS is not only a navigation input; it is a cheap and widely deployed time source, and GNSS-disciplined clocks quietly underpin surveillance feeds, surface-movement and logging across ground estates. A time source that can be walked rather than broken is a category of failure most airport OT inventories have never recorded. One defensive development came out of the same exercise: Splash247 reported on 17 September that ESA tested Galileo’s Signal Authentication Service (SAS), working alongside OSNMA, during Jammertest. Five operational Galileo satellites broadcast encrypted signals for two hours; under spoofing, conventional receivers reported false positions while SAS-equipped receivers detected the interference. Further testing and accreditation come first, and the initial service — free and worldwide — is due in 2027, so this belongs on the receiver roadmap rather than in today’s mitigation. - TechSpot reporting on the Jammertest 2026 exercise at Andøya, with the regulatory backdrop from EASA’s July 2026 jamming and spoofing guidance - Exercise and reporting 10 Sep 2026; Galileo SAS test result reported by Splash247 17 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Recorded Future judges Russia’s hybrid activity in Europe opportunistic but likely to escalate — and an alleged sabotage plot against Leipzig/Halle Airport cargo infrastructure is on its list
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Analytic assessment of hybrid activity; no new aviation cyber incident
item.description: Recorded Future’s Insikt Group published “Russia Escalating Hybrid Attacks across Europe” on 24 September. It assesses that Russia has escalated what Insikt calls New Generation Warfare tactics in Europe since February 2022, describes current activity as “largely opportunistic”, and judges that Russia is likely to escalate over the next two years, potentially culminating in a full-scale campaign. The incidents it cites include an alleged sabotage plot involving explosives against cargo infrastructure at Leipzig/Halle Airport in August 2026, Russian drones in Estonian airspace on 1 September, an explosive maritime drone intercepted near Romania’s Neptun Deep offshore gas field on 20 August, and DDoS and access operations against the Norwegian public sector; Dark Reading’s coverage on 25 September adds water and wastewater targeting in Norway and Poland. This is an analytic assessment, not a report of a new incident, and the attribution to Russia is at assessment level, with no specific unit named. Insikt’s analyst says that “outside of traditional critical infrastructure, logistics and dual-use firms are at high risk.” For aviation the relevance is the mix. A cargo-hub sabotage plot and drone incursions are physical, not cyber, but they land on the same operations centres, perimeter systems and contractor populations that a cyber intrusion would. Insikt’s recommendations — contractor and insider vetting, perimeter detection and anti-drone measures, law-enforcement partnerships, alternative supply routes, coordination with national CERTs and phishing-resistant MFA — read as a checklist for airports and air-cargo operators. - Recorded Future Insikt Group blog; Dark Reading coverage - Insikt blog published 24 Sep 2026; Dark Reading coverage 25 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Two trackers, two August records: NCC Group counts 1,073 ransomware attacks and Comparitech 997 — and a newer group, Aurora, lists transportation among its targets
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Sector statistics from leak-site tracking
item.description: NCC Group’s review of August 2026, reported by Industrial Cyber on 28 September, counted 1,073 ransomware attacks, up 12% on July’s 960, which Industrial Cyber reports as a 2026 high. The industrial sector accounted for 329 attacks, about 31%; North America for 473, about 44%; and Europe for 276, about 26%. Qilin led with 164 attacks, about 15%, overtaking The Gentlemen, and DragonForce was also active. NCC also profiles Aurora, a ransomware-as-a-service group active since late April 2026 that targets manufacturing, legal, research and development and transportation organisations through weak or unauthenticated VPN access and PowerShell credential harvesting, then encrypts hypervisors. Comparitech, reported on 14 September, counted 997 attacks in August, a 23% rise on July’s 809 and above its previous monthly record of 988, with utility, healthcare and business-services attacks behind the rise. The two figures differ because the trackers count differently; both rest on leak-site claims and disclosures, a claimed victim is not a confirmed one, and neither describes confirmed OT downtime. For aviation the useful detail is Aurora’s way in. Weak VPN authentication is exactly the gap that integrator and contractor remote access into airports tends to leave, and encrypting the hypervisor takes down every virtual server on it at once — which is how a back-office ransomware event becomes a check-in, baggage or turnaround outage. - NCC Group monthly ransomware review and Comparitech tracking, both reported by Industrial Cyber - Data for August 2026; NCC review reported 28 Sep 2026; Comparitech figures reported 14 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] Forescout studied 47,700 network segments and found only 13% of those holding OT devices were OT-only — the segmentation question airports tend to assume is already answered
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Network segmentation study; no incident
item.description: Forescout’s Vedere Labs research, published on 22 September and reported by Industrial Cyber on 24 September, analysed 47,700 network segments containing more than 2.5 million devices across 209 organisations. Of the segments that contained OT devices, only 13% were OT-only; the rest also held other types of device, and almost half mixed OT with both IT and IoT assets. Forescout measures the average number of devices per segment as a “blast radius”: 29 in manufacturing and in government, 9 in utilities, 72 in oil and gas and 116 in healthcare. Aviation and transport are not among the sectors it breaks out, and the study describes no incident. Our assessment of the read-across: a terminal network carries BMS, baggage-handling, access-control, CCTV and passenger-facing IoT alongside corporate IT, much of it installed by different integrators at different times, so the finding that OT rarely sits in a segment of its own is a reasonable default assumption until your own inventory proves otherwise. - Forescout Vedere Labs research (22 Sep 2026) — reporting via Industrial Cyber - Reported 24 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Check Point firewalls are being exploited through the VPN handshake, and a separate management-server flaw was in use two months before a fix — both entered KEV on 22 September
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV; federal deadline 25 September passed
item.description: Check Point published a security advisory on 22 September confirming active exploitation of two separate critical flaws. The sources checked for this edition give no CVSS score for either, so none is printed here. The first, CVE-2026-85102, is in Security Gateways and Spark firewalls: improper validation of certificate data during VPN negotiation lets an unauthenticated attacker execute code on the gateway. Check Point released the fix on 9 September and writes that “starting September 12, 2026, we observed a wave of exploitation attempts against Spark customers”; it gives no customer count and no attribution, and publishes indicators in the form of exploitation certificates with the subjects CN=vpn, CN=vpn-user or CN=vpnuser, OU=users, O=global. The second, CVE-2026-93616, is a pre-authentication path traversal in the Security Management web service that leads to script execution or Java class loading. Check Point says it was used in “a handful of pinpointed attacks on July 23, 2026”, about two months before the fix became available on 22 September. It is not CVE-2026-91843, the earlier management-server username flaw, which is still not reported as exploited. CISA added both flaws to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 22 September with a federal deadline of 25 September, in the same batch as Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator and F5 BIG-IP APM. That deadline passed on 25 September. This edition’s research found no further KEV action on either flaw, and no attribution or victim count, as of 6 October. No airport, airline or air navigation service provider has been named as a victim. Our assessment of where it sits in aviation: Spark is Check Point’s small-office firewall line, the class of appliance fitted at outlying sites such as NAVAID and radar shelters, fuel farms, cargo sheds and contractor offices, and often run by a managed-service provider. Check Point gateways also terminate the remote-access VPNs that integrators use to reach terminal BMS, baggage and airfield-lighting systems. The management server is the bigger prize, because it holds the policy for every gateway it manages. - Check Point security advisory of 22 Sep 2026; CISA alert adding four flaws to the KEV catalog, 22 Sep 2026 - CVE-2026-85102 fixed 9 Sep, exploited from 12 Sep; CVE-2026-93616 attacked 23 Jul, fixed 22 Sep; both in KEV 22 Sep 2026, due 25 Sep 2026 (deadline passed); no further KEV action found in this edition’s research

item.title: [Critical] Fortinet’s FortiMail has an exploited CVSS 9.8 flaw that lets an unauthenticated attacker write files to the appliance — in KEV since 1 October, with fixed releases listed in Fortinet’s 5 October update
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV, federal deadline 4 October passed; aviation relevance is our assessment
item.description: Fortinet published PSIRT advisory FG-IR-26-175 on 1 October for CVE-2026-104286 in its FortiMail email security gateway: a path traversal combined with improper handling of NULL bytes that lets an unauthenticated attacker write arbitrary files on the underlying system with crafted HTTP or HTTPS requests. Fortinet scores it CVSS v3 9.8, says it has been reported as exploited in the wild, and found it internally. Affected releases are 7.2.0 to 7.2.9, 7.4.0 to 7.4.8, 7.6.0 to 7.6.6 and 8.0.0 to 8.0.1. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 1 October with a three-day federal deadline of 4 October, which has passed. When the advisory first appeared, fixed releases were planned but undated; Fortinet’s 5 October update lists fixed releases 7.4.9, 7.6.7 and 8.0.2, and tells 7.2 customers to move to the 7.4 branch or later. Fortinet’s workarounds are to disable Identity-Based Encryption (IBE), restrict webmail and management access to trusted networks, and use web-application-firewall rules that block POST requests containing ../ to /ibe paths. No actor, victim or targeted sector has been disclosed. This is not an OT product, and no airport or airline is named. Our assessment of why it is carried: a mail gateway is internet-facing by design, so at an airport authority, airline, ground handler or MRO an unauthenticated file-write flaw on it is a foothold on the corporate edge, and the corporate edge is where the paths into terminal and airfield systems begin. - Fortinet PSIRT advisory FG-IR-26-175 (published 1 Oct 2026, solution updated 5 Oct 2026); CISA KEV catalog; SecurityWeek coverage - KEV listing 1 Oct 2026, due 4 Oct 2026 (passed); fixed releases listed 5 Oct 2026

item.title: [Critical] Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager has an exploited authentication bypass that gives an unauthenticated attacker administrator access — the controller that configures the links to outlying sites
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited zero-day, CISA KEV, federal deadline 3 October passed
item.description: Cisco published advisory cisco-sa-sdwan-webauth-xr8beuuU on 30 September for CVE-2026-76504 in Catalyst SD-WAN Manager, which Cisco rates CVSS 9.8. Improper handling of URI encoding lets a crafted request get past an authentication rule meant to restrict access to a particular API endpoint, giving a remote, unauthenticated attacker administrator-level access. Cisco says its PSIRT became aware of active exploitation in September 2026, and there are no workarounds. Fixed releases are 20.9.10.1, 20.12.8.2, 20.15.6.1, 20.18.4.1, 26.1.2.1 and 26.2.1; anything older than 20.9 has to migrate to a fixed release. Cisco revised the advisory to version 1.1 on 2 October. CISA added the flaw to KEV on 30 September with a 3 October federal deadline, which has passed. BleepingComputer counts it as the fifth exploited Catalyst SD-WAN zero-day of 2026. Cisco names no actor or victim, and no aviation organisation is named. Our assessment of the aviation angle is the same as for Arista’s VeloCloud Orchestrator: the SD-WAN manager is where configuration and policy for every edge router are set, and those edges can connect remote NAVAID and surveillance sites, fuel farms, cargo and MRO facilities and regional airports to the core network. Administrator access to the manager is a view of every site and possibly a way to change how traffic reaches each one. - Cisco security advisory cisco-sa-sdwan-webauth-xr8beuuU (published 30 Sep 2026, revised to v1.1 on 2 Oct 2026); CISA KEV catalog; BleepingComputer coverage - KEV listing 30 Sep 2026, due 3 Oct 2026 (passed); advisory v1.1 2 Oct 2026

item.title: [Critical] MikroTik RouterOS: three exploited flaws in KEV, and now a CVSS 9.8 pre-authentication web-management flaw from CISA that is not reported exploited
item.category: Critical Advisory — Three RouterOS flaws exploited and in CISA KEV; CVE-2026-84411 in a CISA ICS advisory of 29 September, not in KEV
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-67279 in MikroTik RouterOS to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 25 September, with a federal deadline of 28 September. KEV describes it as improper enforcement of a behavioural workflow in SSH that “could allow an unauthenticated client to open a session channel and send an exec request,” and notes that it can be chained to exploit CVE-2026-86060 without authentication. Coverage rates it CVSS 6.9, with no scoring version stated. It joins two RouterOS flaws CISA added on 10 September: CVE-2026-86060, an argument-injection flaw, and CVE-2026-67277, a missing-authentication flaw in the bandwidth-test service. CERT Polska’s posts of 5 September reported in-the-wild exploitation, from about 2 September, of a two-flaw SSH chain it calls “MikroTrick”. CERT Polska’s 22 September technical analysis names the chain: CVE-2026-67279 combined with CVE-2026-86060, which gives an unauthenticated attacker full administrative control. CVE-2026-67276, which earlier coverage tied to the chain, is not in KEV. Fixed builds are RouterOS 7.24.2, 7.23.4 and 6.49.21; the related CVE-2026-67278 needs 7.24.3 or 7.23.6, because the earlier fix was incomplete. Shadowserver counted more than 122,500 MikroTik devices with SSH reachable from the internet in early September; that is an exposure count, not a count of unpatched or compromised devices. No victims, sectors or actor have been named. The aviation relevance is breadth rather than any confirmed airport targeting: RouterOS boxes turn up in the inexpensive, quietly installed corners of an airport estate — remote stands and cargo sheds, car parks and shuttle depots, contractor site offices, CCTV and Wi-Fi backhaul — the places least likely to appear in an asset register and most likely to have an SSH port open for vendor support. Update, 29 September: CISA published ICS advisory ICSA-26-272-06 for a separate RouterOS flaw, CVE-2026-84411, a pre-authentication integer underflow in the web management interface that can lead to code execution or denial of service, rated CVSS v3.1 9.8 and v4 9.3. RouterOS before 7.24 is affected, and CISA lists 7.24 or later as fixed. It is not in KEV, no exploitation has been reported, and it is not part of the chain CERT Polska named. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog; CERT Polska posts of 5 Sep 2026; The Hacker News coverage of the 25 Sep KEV addition; CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-272-06 - CERT Polska 5 Sep 2026; KEV additions 10 Sep 2026 and 25 Sep 2026 (CVE-2026-67279 due 28 Sep 2026, passed); ICSA-26-272-06 (CVE-2026-84411) published 29 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] A CVSS 10 command-injection flaw in VIVOTEK camera firmware covers 37 models and already has public proof-of-concept code — CISA lists Transportation Systems among the sectors that use them
item.category: Critical Advisory — CISA ICSA-26-272-03; public proof-of-concept; no known exploitation; aviation relevance is our assessment
item.description: CISA published ICSA-26-272-03 on 29 September for CVE-2026-22755, a command-injection flaw in VIVOTEK IP camera firmware affecting 37 camera models. It is rated CVSS v3.1 10.0 and v4 9.3, and public proof-of-concept code exists. The remedy is the latest firmware for each model. CISA lists Government Services and Facilities, Transportation Systems, Commercial Facilities, Energy, Critical Manufacturing and Financial Services among the sectors concerned, and reports no known exploitation. Nothing in the advisory names an airport. Our assessment of why it belongs here: IP cameras are among the most numerous networked devices on an airport estate, in terminals, car parks, cargo areas, aprons and along the perimeter, and they are usually installed and maintained by a security integrator rather than by IT. Public exploit code for a maximum-severity flaw shortens the time before someone scans for them, and a compromised camera is a foothold on the video network, which often shares cabling and switches with access control. The same 29 September batch of seven advisories also covered the Lantronix G520 cellular gateway, a new MikroTik RouterOS flaw, Toptech TMS7 and TopHAT terminal software, and three products for which no fix is planned: a Baicells LTE base station, an Anjvision product and the Viidure dashcam app. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-272-03, read from CISA’s machine-readable advisory data - Advisory published 29 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] CISA’s 1 October batch reaches terminal building systems: Armatura One access control ships an ActiveMQ flaw already exploited elsewhere, and Johnson Controls EasyIO building controllers get two fixes
item.category: Advisory — CISA ICS batch, 1 October; no known exploitation; aviation relevance is our assessment
item.description: CISA released six ICS advisories on 1 October, ICSA-26-274-01 to -06, and two cover building systems of the kind found in terminals. Armatura One, a physical access-control platform (-01), embeds a version of Apache ActiveMQ vulnerable to CVE-2023-46604, rated CVSS v3.1 9.8 and v4 10.0. That flaw is already in CISA’s KEV catalog because it was exploited against other ActiveMQ deployments, including by ransomware actors; CISA reports no exploitation of Armatura One itself. The same advisory lists a hard-coded cryptographic key (CVE-2026-94591) and hard-coded credentials (CVE-2026-94592), both 8.4 under v3.1 and 8.6 under v4, a log-exposure flaw (CVE-2026-94593, 7.8 and 8.5) and a lower-rated issue (CVE-2026-94594, 4.0). Versions before 4.7.2, and USA builds before 4.6.1, are affected; the fixes are 4.7.2 and 4.6.1_USA. CISA lists Transportation Systems among the sectors. Johnson Controls EasyIO Neo EC and CW building controllers (-04 and -05) have an information-exposure flaw, CVE-2026-64892 (3.5 under v3.1, 6.3 under v4), and cleartext transmission of sensitive data, CVE-2026-64893 (5.4 and 7.3), fixed in EC V3.3b64 and CW V3.3b26; CISA again lists Transportation Systems. The rest of the batch: Monta’s EV-charging platform (-02), whose missing authentication on a WebSocket channel, CVE-2026-95102 (9.4 under v3.1, 9.3 under v4), allows charging-station impersonation and has no fixed version, only configuration guidance — Monta points to OCPP 1.6 Security Profile 2 and says rate limiting is in place; ABB PCM600 up to 2.14 (-03), with a privilege-escalation and a path-traversal flaw, a workaround and no fixed version; and the Meari IoT cloud platform (-06), with no fix planned. CISA reports no known exploitation for any of the six. No airport is named. Our assessment: access control and building management are airport OT in everything but name, usually run by facilities and security contractors, and an access-control server with hard-coded keys and credentials is a direct route to doors, turnstiles and badge records. EV chargers appear in airport car parks and electric ground-support fleets, which is why the Monta item is listed here. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-274-01 to -06, read from CISA’s machine-readable advisory data and CISA’s 1 Oct bulletin - Advisories published 1 Oct 2026

item.title: [Medium] A signature-check flaw in Lantronix G520 cellular gateways could let an attacker replace the software and run code as root — the kind of box that connects an airport’s outlying sites
item.category: Advisory — CISA ICSA-26-272-01, Transportation Systems listed; no known exploitation
item.description: CISA published ICSA-26-272-01 on 29 September for two flaws in Lantronix G520 Series cellular gateways running 2.6.0.4R6_stable: CVE-2026-91191, improper verification of a cryptographic signature, and CVE-2026-84409, a cross-site scripting flaw, each rated CVSS v3.1 7.5 and v4 7.7. CISA says exploitation could allow an attacker to replace software and execute arbitrary code with root privileges. The fix is release 2.6.0.7R6. CISA lists Transportation Systems, Energy, and Water and Wastewater as the sectors concerned and reports no known exploitation. No airport or airline is named. Our assessment of the aviation angle: cellular gateways are how sites without fixed lines get connected, and on an airport estate that tends to mean the edges — car-park pay stations and barriers, remote stands, fuel-farm and pump-station telemetry, construction compounds and contractor remote-support links — often installed by whoever built the site and missing from the network inventory. A gateway that accepts replaced software is a persistent foothold at exactly the places least watched. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-272-01, read from CISA’s machine-readable advisory data - Advisory published 29 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Arista’s VeloCloud SD-WAN orchestrator has a CVSS 10 flaw under active attack — the console that configures the links to your outlying sites
item.category: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV, federal deadline 25 September
item.description: Arista published Security Advisory 0183 on 22 September for CVE-2026-93952, an improper input validation flaw in on-premises VeloCloud Orchestrator (VCO), rated CVSS 10.0 under v3.1 and 9.5 under v4.0. Arista says the flaw “may allow a remote attacker to access privileged internal functionality and impact the VCO host” and that it is “known to be actively exploited.” Exposure depends on configuration. An attacker needs certificate-based authentication to be set up between VeloCloud Edges and the orchestrator, the public part of an Edge’s authentication certificate, and network access to the VCO web interface; “VCO tenant or operator credentials are not required.” Vulnerable on-prem releases are 5.2.3.15 and earlier, 6.1.3.7 and earlier, 6.4.2.7 and earlier, and 7.0.0.2 and earlier. Fixes are in 5.2.3.16 and 6.4.2.8, and at publication Arista listed no fixed build for the 6.1 or 7.0 trains; check the advisory for later releases. Hosted and dedicated VCO instances have already been patched. Arista publishes indicators: the files /usr/local/sbin/.vcnode.js and /usr/local/sbin/vc-sysmond (MD5 dc78e206eaeadec59fc5801fe4556bd0), a vc-sysmon systemd service, an x-vc-opt HTTP header, and the source addresses 142.93.149.77 and 104.248.126.159. CISA added the flaw to KEV on 22 September with a 25 September deadline. No aviation victim is named. The aviation angle is architectural. An SD-WAN orchestrator pushes configuration and policy to every edge it manages, and those edges can connect remote NAVAID and surveillance sites, fuel farms, cargo and MRO facilities, and regional airports to the core network. Compromising the orchestrator gives an attacker a view of every site and possibly a way into each one. - Arista Security Advisory 0183, read from Arista’s advisory page; CISA alert adding four flaws to the KEV catalog, 22 Sep 2026 - Advisory and KEV listing 22 Sep 2026; federal deadline 25 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] An F5 BIG-IP APM overflow gives unauthenticated code execution, but only where APM acts as an OAuth authorisation server — and it is being exploited
item.category: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV, federal deadline 25 September
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-94127 in F5 BIG-IP Access Policy Manager to the KEV catalog on 22 September, with a federal deadline of 25 September. The flaw is a heap-based buffer overflow rated CVSS 9.8 under v3.1 and 9.3 under v4.0 that allows unauthenticated remote code execution. It is covered by F5 advisory K000162605. Exposure is narrower than the score suggests. Rapid7’s analysis says a system is exposed only when a virtual server has both an APM access policy and an OAuth profile attached, so that APM is acting as an OAuth authorisation server. F5 has issued engineering hotfixes for the 21.1.0, 17.5.0 and 17.1.0 branches. Rapid7 reported no confirmed public proof-of-concept as of 22 September, and F5 has published no attribution or victim count. No aviation victim is named. It belongs on this page because BIG-IP APM is widely used as the access gateway in front of web portals and vendor remote access, the role it can play for crew, engineering and MRO applications and for integrator access into airport systems, and in an OAuth-server role it issues the tokens those applications trust. - CISA alert adding four flaws to the KEV catalog, 22 Sep 2026; Rapid7 emergent-threat analysis of 22 Sep 2026, citing F5 advisory K000162605 - KEV listing 22 Sep 2026; federal deadline 25 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Cisco’s network access control server has a CVSS 10 authentication bypass under active attack — this is the box that decides which devices get onto which airport network
item.category: Advisory — Actively exploited zero-day, CISA KEV
item.description: Cisco published advisory cisco-sa-ISE-ABP-VNSW7Tn5 on 16 September for CVE-2026-76460, a CVSS 10.0 flaw in Identity Services Engine and ISE-PIC that lets an unauthenticated remote attacker bypass the web-based management interface through an API endpoint with insufficient authentication. Cisco states its PSIRT “is aware of active exploitation of this vulnerability.” All versions are affected; fixes are 3.1 Patch 12, 3.2 Patch 11, 3.3 Patch 12, 3.4 Patch 7 and 3.5 Patch 4. There are no workarounds — restricting management traffic with infrastructure access control lists is the only mitigation short of patching. CISA added the CVE to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 16 September with an unusually short three-day federal remediation deadline of 19 September, which has now passed. No attribution has been published and no critical-infrastructure or aviation targeting has been claimed; Singapore’s Cyber Security Agency issued its own alert on 21 September urging immediate patching. The reason it matters here is architectural rather than reported: where an airport or airline estate runs 802.1X and posture-based access control, ISE is the policy engine that decides which contractor laptop, handheld or engineering workstation lands on a terminal, baggage or airside VLAN — so administrative control of it is control of the segmentation itself. - Cisco security advisory cisco-sa-ISE-ABP-VNSW7Tn5 and the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog — corroborated by SecurityWeek and BleepingComputer - Cisco advisory published 16 Sep 2026; added to CISA KEV 16 Sep 2026, deadline 19 Sep 2026, now passed; CSA Singapore alert 21 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] A Zyxel small-office switch flaw enters KEV after 996 devices in 48 countries were harvested for configurations and credentials — the kit in the corners of an airport nobody inventories
item.category: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV, federal deadline 24 September
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-7273 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 21 September with a federal remediation deadline of 24 September. The flaw is a stack-based buffer overflow in the CGI program of Zyxel’s GS1900-series managed switches — GS1900-8, 8HP, 10HP, 16, 24, 24E, 24EP, 24HPv2, 48 and 48HPv2 — that lets an unauthenticated attacker on the LAN execute operating-system commands with a crafted HTTP request; Zyxel patched it on 16 June in firmware 2.90(AAHH.2)C0 and per-model equivalents, and publishes no CVSS score for it. GreyNoise research published on 21 September documents what it describes as the first in-the-wild exploitation: a single actor assessed as Chinese-speaking compromised 996 GS1900 switches across 48 countries from about mid-August — Italy, the United States, Taiwan, France, South Korea and the Netherlands lead the count — using an obfuscated Python tool that pulled device configurations and root-level hashed credentials over TFTP; 564 of the victims were still on factory-default credentials. The same actor stole records from an unnamed western government organisation through two WordPress flaws and also targeted Gitea CVE-2026-60004, among other products; GreyNoise describes the switch actor as “the same or related to” the group Acronis calls Red Heron, based on shared infrastructure, malware and tactics; treat that as GreyNoise’s assessment rather than a confirmed attribution. KEV lists the flaw as LAN-based, so the practical exposure is any path that reaches the switch’s management interface. That is the aviation angle: GS1900-class switches are what a contractor site office, a car-park attendant booth, a retail concession or a CCTV closet gets fitted with, they rarely appear in an asset register, and a stolen configuration is a map of every VLAN the switch carries plus the credentials to reach it. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog entry of 21 Sep 2026, GreyNoise research published 21 Sep 2026 and Zyxel’s security advisory for the GS1900 series of 16 Jun 2026 - Zyxel advisory 16 Jun 2026; KEV listing 21 Sep 2026; GreyNoise research published 21 Sep 2026; federal deadline 24 Sep 2026, passed

item.title: [Critical] An APT cluster whose tooling overlaps Sandworm and a ransomware operator that deployed Qilin are exploiting Cisco firewall management — the boundary between airport IT and airfield OT
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed
item.description: Cisco and CISA confirmed on 9 September that CVE-2026-20079 in Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center is being exploited in the wild. The flaw is a critical authentication bypass caused by an improper system process created at boot; a remote, unauthenticated attacker sends crafted HTTP requests and gains root on the underlying operating system. Cisco patched it in early March and added indicators of compromise in late July, then disclosed on 9 September that it had observed exploitation from August. CISA added the CVE to its KEV catalog with a 12 September federal deadline, which has now passed. Cisco Talos tracks three post-compromise clusters across this flaw and the earlier static-credential flaw CVE-2026-20316: UAT-12197, unattributed, which used CVE-2026-20079 to plant a web shell and a JAR-based command executor and exfiltrate credentials; UAT-11823, an APT that used both CVEs and whose tooling Talos says overlaps with Sandworm’s, deploying Cyclops Blink — Talos does not say Sandworm itself carried out the activity; and UAT-11988, which Talos assesses with high confidence to be a ransomware operator with TTPs consistent with Qilin affiliates, came in through CVE-2026-20316 alone, enumerated targets for encryption and deployed Qilin on selected endpoints. CVE-2026-20316 is not in the KEV catalogue. Talos last updated its post on 21 September, and no new development has been reported as of 27 September. On 16 September Cisco shipped its September hardening release for ASA, FTD and FMC (CVE-2026-20329 to CVE-2026-20336, maximum CVSS 9.9), which accompanies the exploited FMC flaws. Airports should treat this as an airfield-and-terminal segmentation problem rather than an office IT patch. The firewalls FMC configures are usually what stands between the corporate network and baggage handling, jet bridges, fuelling, de-icing, airfield lighting, BMS and access control. - Cisco security advisory update and Cisco Talos research of 9 Sep 2026, plus the CISA KEV addition of 9 Sep 2026 — reported by SecurityWeek - Advisory updated and KEV listing added 9 Sep 2026; reporting 10 Sep 2026; hardening release published 16 Sep 2026; KEV status re-checked 21 Sep 2026; KEV federal deadline of 12 Sep 2026 now passed

item.title: [Critical] NetScaler is being probed harder than it is being patched — 56 exploitation attempts in a week against an authentication bypass now in KEV
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-19490 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 9 September, an authentication bypass rated CVSS 9.3 affecting Citrix NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway in AAA virtual server and Gateway configurations, with a federal deadline of 12 September that has now passed. Honeypot telemetry logged 56 exploitation attempts from 3 September onward, 36 of them on 8 September alone, which is the shape of opportunistic mass scanning rather than targeted intrusion — internet-facing devices are being found and tried before their owners finish the change window. It arrived in the same KEV batch as the Fortinet FortiOS, FortiSwitchManager and FortiSASE heap overflow CVE-2025-25249, exploited since July and linked to a campaign that has infected an estimated 178 FortiGate devices with the PivotC2 remote access trojan. Aviation reads these as one exposure. NetScaler Gateway is a common front door for airline crew and operations portals, engineering and MRO applications and third-party access into terminal systems, and FortiGate is among the most common devices sitting on the boundary between an airport’s corporate network and its airside estate. An authentication bypass on either is not a data-theft problem, it is a segmentation problem. Separately, Citrix has since patched three further exploited NetScaler zero-days, CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772 on 27 September and CVE-2026-88779 days later; they are distinct from CVE-2026-19490 — see the top story. - CISA KEV additions of 9 Sep 2026 for Citrix NetScaler and Fortinet FortiOS, reported by The Hacker News with honeypot exploitation telemetry - KEV listings 9 Sep 2026; federal deadline 12 Sep 2026, now passed; Fortinet exploitation traced to Jul 2026

item.title: [Critical] ScreenConnect is being used to push scripts to endpoints as they connect — the console your handlers and integrators already have on your estate
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-84869 in ConnectWise ScreenConnect to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 12 September with a federal remediation deadline of 14 September. The flaw is a missing authorisation check rated CVSS 9.9 that permits unauthorised file transfer and code execution, and three separate incidents have been documented in which threat actors abused it to push malicious scripts to endpoints as those endpoints newly connected to a server. That detail is the one that matters operationally: the malicious action arrives through the legitimate management channel, signed off by the tool the estate is built to trust, so it looks like maintenance rather than intrusion. ScreenConnect and its peers are the standing path by which ground handlers, baggage and BMS maintainers, access-control contractors and airport systems integrators reach terminal systems out of hours, frequently on instances the airport authority neither owns nor patches. It sits alongside the month’s other confirmed remote-access exploitation as a single theme: the attacker is no longer forcing a boundary, they are borrowing the support tool that already crosses it. - CISA KEV catalog addition of 12 Sep 2026, reported by The Hacker News alongside the Artifactory and RouterOS additions in the same batch - KEV listing 12 Sep 2026; federal deadline 14 Sep 2026, now passed

item.title: [Critical] GitLab CVSS 10 path traversal is being exploited, and airport and airline teams host more of it than they think
item.category: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV
item.description: GitLab patched CVE-2026-85706 on 10 September, a path-traversal flaw in the repository commits API that it rated CVSS 10.0 and that allows an unauthenticated attacker to read arbitrary files from a GitLab server. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Friday 11 September with a remediation deadline for federal agencies of Monday 14 September. watchTowr reported it was already seeing in-the-wild probes for vulnerable servers, and Hong Kong’s CERT issued its own advisory on 14 September stating the flaw is being exploited in the wild. A second flaw fixed in the same release, CVE-2026-87719, can expose sensitive information from Enterprise Edition servers. Airport and airline estates version baggage-handling integrations, gate and stand allocation logic, BMS and access-control middleware, MRO systems and airline operations tooling in self-hosted GitLab. Unauthenticated file reads against those servers surface the service accounts and API keys that reach airside and terminal systems. - GitLab patch release advisory and CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog — reporting via Cybersecurity Dive - GitLab patch published 10 Sep 2026; KEV listing 11 Sep 2026; reporting 14 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Twenty flaws in Pepperl+Fuchs IO-Link masters, two at CVSS 9.8 — and the same firmware ships under Phoenix Contact and Carlo Gavazzi badges
item.category: Advisory — CERT@VDE VDE-2026-014; no known exploitation
item.description: CERT@VDE published VDE-2026-014 on 16 September: Pepperl+Fuchs has fixed 20 vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-27546 to CVE-2026-27565, in the firmware of its ICE2-8IOL and ICE3-8IOL IO-Link master modules, found by Nozomi Networks Labs researchers, with the fix in firmware 1.7.8. The two worst are CVE-2026-27546, an authentication bypass, and CVE-2026-27565, unauthenticated upload of a malicious IODD device-description file that executes shell scripts, both at CVSS 9.8. Most of the rest, CVE-2026-27547 through -27564, are command-injection, file-inclusion and authorisation flaws between 7.2 and 8.8 that lead to root-level code execution on the module; CVE-2026-27557 at 7.5 is an unauthenticated path traversal that reads the module’s SSH server private keys, and CVE-2026-27553 at 6.5 discloses password hashes. The same firmware is sold rebadged, so the exposure is wider than one vendor: Phoenix Contact IOL MA8 PN DI8 and IOL MA8 EIP DI8 masters carry the same 20 CVEs under VDE-2026-027, and Carlo Gavazzi YL212 and YN115 masters are covered by VDE-2026-028, all with the same 1.7.8 fix and the same date. Nozomi Networks Labs published its own technical write-up on 24 September, covering 19 of the CVEs on the ICE2-8IOL-K45P-RJ45 and describing how, chained, they give an unauthenticated attacker root on the module and the ability to manipulate sensor and actuator data. No exploitation is reported, and the flaws did not appear in CISA’s ICS advisory batches through 24 September. Our assessment of the aviation relevance, since no airport is named: IO-Link is the sensor and actuator layer of modern conveyor and sortation systems, and baggage-handling systems are assembled by integrators from exactly this class of discrete-automation component. A master module that gives root to anyone who can reach its web interface is a foothold on the PROFINET or EtherNet/IP segment that runs the belts. - CERT@VDE advisory VDE-2026-014, with Nozomi Networks Labs research credit and CVE records at MITRE; rebadged products per VDE-2026-027 and VDE-2026-028; Nozomi Networks Labs technical write-up - Advisories published 16 Sep 2026; Nozomi write-up 24 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Six flaws in Digital Watchdog VMAX video recorders, the top two at CVSS 9.6 — CISA lists Transportation Systems among the sectors that run them
item.category: Advisory — CISA ICSA-26-258-01, Transportation Systems listed
item.description: CISA published ICSA-26-258-01 on 15 September covering Digital Watchdog VMAX digital and network video recorders — the A1 G4, IP G4, A1 PLUS, VA1G4 and VG4 lines. Six CVEs are listed, led by CVE-2026-66890 and CVE-2026-66887 at CVSS 9.6, with CVE-2026-68070 and CVE-2026-68950 at 8.8 and two lower-rated issues at 6.8 and 6.5. CISA states that exploitation can give an attacker full administrative control of the recorder. Updated firmware is available from the vendor, and no exploitation has been reported. The sectors CISA names for this advisory are Commercial Facilities, Government Services and Facilities, Healthcare and Public Health, and Transportation Systems. That last one is why it is carried here: recorders of this class are ordinary physical-security infrastructure in terminals, car parks, cargo sheds and landside offices, they are frequently installed and maintained by a security integrator rather than by IT, and they sit on cabling that often runs into the same closets as access control. Nothing in the advisory names an airport — treat this as an inventory question, not an aviation incident. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-258-01, read from the CISA CSAF advisory feed - Advisory published 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] CISA’s 22 September batch brings nine advisories, and two of them are airport-terminal systems: Siemens Desigo CC building management and Siveillance Control security management
item.category: Advisory — CISA ICS batch, 22 September
item.description: CISA released nine ICS advisories on Tuesday 22 September, ICSA-26-265-01 through -09. Two cover the lwIP embedded TCP/IP stack: an out-of-bounds write in its MQTT client application, reported by Shahriyar Jalayeri of ByteRay (-01), and a double free, reported by Eric Evenchick of Tetrel Security (-02). Six are Siemens: Siveillance Control, an unrestricted upload of a file with a dangerous type (-03); SIPLUS and SIMATIC products affected by the third-party Linux “Copy Fail” flaw (-04); the Desigo CC family, a code injection reported by Michelin CERT (-05); Industrial Edge Management, a third-party weak password-recovery issue (-06); SIMOVE Fleetmanager and SIPLANT, a relative path traversal (-07); and WTV676 and WTV776, improper validation of a specified type of input (-08). The last is OpenPLC, a cross-site scripting flaw (-09). For this page, two of those matter most. Desigo CC is Siemens’ building-management platform and sits over HVAC, fire and energy systems in many terminals. Siveillance Control is a security-management platform that brings access control, video and alarms together in a control room. We could not reach CISA’s own advisory pages at generation time. CVE numbers, CVSS scores, fix availability and CISA’s sector listings are therefore deliberately left out rather than taken from secondary digests; read each advisory before prioritising. No exploitation has been reported for anything in the batch. Update for this edition: the lwIP MQTT advisory (-01) is now verified from CISA’s advisory data as CVE-2026-87121, rated CVSS v3.1 9.8 and v4 9.3, in lwIP MQTT 2.0.1 to 2.2.1; it was not in KEV as of 1 October. The other eight advisories remain as described above. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-265-01 to -09, product and vulnerability-type list confirmed from the Chemical Facility Security News review of 22 Sep 2026; lwIP (-01) CVE and scores later verified from CISA’s advisory data - Advisories published 22 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Nozomi finishes its Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403 research: twelve flaws, several chainable to root on an OT edge device — patched, unexploited, and older than it looks
item.category: Research — Vendor-patched, no known exploitation
item.description: Correction to the previous edition. This entry previously read as a new critical disclosure dated 15 September. It was not. The underlying CVEs were disclosed in May 2025 under CISA advisory ICSA-25-135-18; what happened on 15 September was a CISA update to that advisory, adding the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client and vendor fixes. The research behind it published in two parts: the first, on 10 September, covered four PROFINET Discovery and basic Configuration Protocol memory-corruption flaws in the SCALANCE LPE9403 — an uninitialised value, a NULL pointer dereference and two out-of-bounds reads, each rated CVSS 5.3 and each a denial of service rather than code execution. The second part, published by Nozomi Networks Labs on 18 September, gives the full picture: twelve vulnerabilities in total, nine in the device firmware rated between 5.3 and 8.5 and three in the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client rated between 6.7 and 8.5. Nozomi demonstrated that several of them can be chained to obtain root-level control of the device, which in an OT context means manipulating telemetry, suppressing alarms, reading operational data, disrupting services and moving laterally. Affected are LPE9403 firmware below V4.0 HF0 and the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client through V2.1; Siemens has published advisories and fixes, with V4.0 HF0 and later the fixed firmware. There is no evidence of exploitation in the wild. For aviation the relevance is where these devices sit: the LPE9403 is a local-processing engine used as a PROFINET edge collector, and where an integrator has put one into baggage, plant-room, BMS or airfield equipment, root on it is root inside the segment that equipment lives in. - Nozomi Networks Labs research, Siemens ProductCERT SSA-327438 and CISA advisory ICSA-25-135-18 — reporting via Industrial Cyber - CVEs disclosed May 2025; research published 10 and 18 Sep 2026; CISA advisory updated 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Rockwell extends its lock-out recovery guidance to Micro820 and Micro850 — the small PLCs in the parts of an airport that never get a security review
item.category: Guidance — Rockwell Automation SD1790 revision 5.0; exploitation is the premise, per the FBI
item.description: Rockwell Automation revised security notice SD1790 for a fifth time on 18 September. The notice, first published on 30 July, is titled as hardening guidance and instructions for restoring access when a controller’s password is unknown, and revision 5.0 extends the recovery and hardening instructions to Micro820 and Micro850 controllers alongside the MicroLogix 1100 and 1400 it already covered. It exists because of the FBI’s public service announcement of 30 July, which described attackers remotely altering the configuration of internet-exposed PLCs, changing IP addresses and setting passwords where none had existed, locking operators out of their own controllers. There is no CVE; the guidance is to remove controllers from direct internet exposure, reach them through a VPN and firewall isolation, set strong passwords, keep offline project backups, disable the controller’s HTTP server and keep firmware current. Revision 5.0 adds no new incident data and names no sector; Rockwell has published no new vulnerability advisories since its 1 September batch. Our assessment of why it belongs here: MicroLogix and Micro800 controllers are the PLCs of small standalone plant — car-park barriers and pay-on-foot systems, pump stations, fuel-farm ancillaries, de-icing fluid recovery, packaged HVAC — typically installed by a mechanical or electrical contractor with a cellular router for remote support, and typically absent from the airport’s own asset register. The FBI’s scenario, a controller that suddenly has a password its owner does not know, is the one those sites are least prepared to recover from. - Rockwell Automation security notice SD1790, revision 5.0, read from Rockwell’s trust center; FBI public service announcement of 30 Jul 2026 as referenced by the notice - Notice first published 30 Jul 2026; revision 5.0 published 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Moxa fixes an unauthenticated crash in the web login of its TN-4500B switches — a rolling-stock line, so the airport question is the people-mover
item.category: Advisory — Moxa MPSA-252620; no known exploitation
item.description: Moxa published security advisory MPSA-252620 on 18 September for CVE-2026-15579 in its TN-4500B Ethernet switch series, a line Moxa’s product page describes as designed for railway applications including rolling stock and as meeting EN 50155 test requirements. The flaw is an out-of-bounds write in the web login: the username field is not length-checked, so a remote, unauthenticated attacker who can reach the web interface can send an overlong value and crash the authentication process. Moxa describes the impact as denial of service with no confidentiality loss, scores it CVSS v4 8.8 and rates it High. Firmware v2.0 and earlier is affected; v2.1 or later fixes it. The advisory makes no statement about exploitation and we found no report of attacks. This is not an airport product and we have no evidence of it at any airport. It is carried because the one place a rolling-stock switch does turn up on an airport estate is the automated people-mover or airside shuttle, which is usually maintained by a rail systems contractor under a separate contract and separate security regime from the terminal. If you have no people-mover, file this; if you do, the question is whether the on-board network’s web management is reachable from the train-to-ground link or from the maintenance depot network. - Moxa security advisory MPSA-252620 and the Moxa TN-4500B product page - Published 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] GAO finds only 7 of 22 civilian agencies fully meet federal rules for managing networked IoT and OT devices — and an industry coalition now asks CISA for a binding OT directive
item.category: Regulation & Policy — GAO audit of federal IoT and OT device management; industry proposal for a CISA directive (proposal only)
item.description: GAO-26-108937, published on 30 September, reviewed how 22 civilian CFO Act agencies manage networked Internet of Things and OT devices against OMB requirements that date from December 2023, were updated in January 2025 and carried a September 2024 completion deadline. Fifteen agencies had established device inventories, 11 maintained them, 10 included all the required information, and only seven fully met all three requirements. No agency reported an IoT cybersecurity waiver. GAO notes that OMB has not issued updated guidance covering fiscal year 2026 and makes one recommendation: that OMB issue updated guidance covering networked IoT and OT devices and oversee its implementation. On 6 October CyberScoop reported that the OT Cybersecurity Coalition is urging CISA to issue a binding operational directive focused solely on OT security at federal agencies, citing the GAO findings and this summer’s water-utility attacks. The coalition wants an accountable OT cybersecurity officer at each agency, minimum practices drawn from existing federal guidance, alignment with CISA’s 2022 Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals, and a review of whether NSA’s OT guidance should apply to civilian agencies. This is a proposal only. CISA has announced no directive and did not respond to CyberScoop. For aviation readers the relevance is indirect. GAO’s numbers show how hard it is to keep even an inventory of networked devices current, which is the same first step airport OT programmes struggle with, and a federal OT directive, if one were issued, would become a public reference point for what a minimum OT programme looks like. - GAO-26-108937, read from GAO’s product page; CyberScoop reporting on the OT Cybersecurity Coalition’s proposal - GAO report published 30 Sep 2026; coalition proposal reported 6 Oct 2026

item.title: [Info] GAO’s industry panel says overlapping federal cyber-reporting rules can pull responders away from the incident — and the CIRCIA final rule has missed its September target
item.category: Regulation & Policy — GAO report on overlapping cyber regulations; CIRCIA final rule still unpublished
item.description: The Government Accountability Office published GAO-26-109197, “Cybersecurity Regulations: Industry Panelists Identify Duplication and Conflicts and Ways to Address Them”, on 28 September. It reports a virtual panel held on 16 July with six industry representatives from energy, financial services, and healthcare and public health. Panelists said it could be hard to meet every reporting requirement while also remediating a cyber threat, saw DHS and SEC rules as duplicating sector rules, and half of them agreed that progress on harmonisation had been limited. Their suggestions were consistent timeframes, thresholds and definitions; a lead agency such as CISA to coordinate reporting; and closer government–industry collaboration. The report makes no formal recommendations, and transportation was not on the panel. Separately, the final rule under the Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act (CIRCIA) had still not appeared in the Federal Register at generation time; the federal regulatory agenda had targeted September 2026. Once in force it would require covered incidents to be reported within 72 hours and ransom payments within 24 hours; any text quoted today as the rule is the 2024 proposal. For aviation the relevance is practical: airports, airlines and their service providers can answer to several regulators for the same incident, and the harmonisation question the panel raised is the one an incident team meets in its first hours. - GAO-26-109197, read from GAO’s product page; Federal Register check for the CIRCIA final rule; Cybersecurity Dive and Infosecurity Magazine coverage - GAO report published 28 Sep 2026; CIRCIA final rule not in the Federal Register at generation time

item.title: [Info] CISA’s Cybersecurity Awareness Month campaign, “Securing the Next 250”, asks operators to reduce, replace and recover — and replacing end-of-support kit is the hard part for airport OT
item.category: Regulation & Policy — CISA awareness campaign; voluntary, not a rule
item.description: CISA launched “Securing the Next 250” at the start of Cybersecurity Awareness Month, as reported by Industrial Cyber on 2 October. The campaign frames its advice for organisations as three Rs: reduce attack surfaces, replace end-of-support devices, and recover quickly to keep operations running. For individuals it repeats four practices: avoid and report phishing, use strong passwords, use multifactor authentication with a password manager, and keep software updated. Acting Director Nick Andersen tied the campaign to the knock-on effect of disruption: when critical infrastructure fails, the businesses and communities that depend on it fail with it. It is a voluntary awareness campaign, not a rule or directive, and it sets no sector-specific requirement. For airports the useful part is the middle R. Terminal OT often includes devices past their support life — ageing BMS front ends, baggage-control workstations, access-control servers and controllers fitted at construction — and replacing them runs on capital-project timescales, not patch cycles. - CISA campaign, reported by Industrial Cyber (CISA’s own page not fetched at generation time) - Campaign launched at the start of October 2026; reported 2 Oct 2026

item.title: [Info] CISA and FBI on integrator risk: one compromised automation vendor, about 800 files of its customers’ SCADA details — and transportation among those customers
item.category: Guidance — CISA and FBI joint fact sheet on third-party ICS integrator risk; the cited 2025 case involved an integrator serving power utilities and transportation entities; no CVE
item.description: CISA and the FBI publicised a joint fact sheet on 24 September, Considerations for Critical Infrastructure Operators Working With Third-Party ICS Integrators; the document itself is dated 23 September. It cites a case in which foreign cyber actors, between March and April 2025, compromised a US industrial automation company that provided system integration, engineering consulting and SCADA programming services to customers including power utilities and transportation entities. On the integrator’s network the actors searched for terms including “customers” and “SCADA” and packaged approximately 800 files — customer SCADA information, ICS device details and schematics — into nine archive files. The fact sheet names neither the integrator, its customers nor the actor, and describes no disruption. Its recommendations are least privilege for every integrator connection, on-demand remote access that the operator authorises and can monitor, and contract terms covering data storage, remote access and patching. No airport, airline or air navigation service provider is named, and this is guidance, not a new incident. It is carried here because airport ground OT is among the most integrator-dependent estates in transport: baggage handling, jet bridges, airfield lighting, fuel systems and terminal BMS are typically installed and supported by a specialist integrator who holds the drawings, the configurations and a standing way in — the same asset class the 2025 case shows is worth stealing even when the operator’s own network is never touched. - CISA and FBI joint fact sheet (dated 23 Sep 2026, publicised 24 Sep 2026); reported by Industrial Cyber and SecurityWeek - Publicised 24 Sep 2026 — case details verified against Industrial Cyber and the FBI-hosted PDF

item.title: [Info] NIST opens its OT security guide for revision: the SP 800-82 Rev. 4 draft expands to building automation and industrial IoT, with comments due 30 November
item.category: Regulation & Policy — Draft guidance open for comment
item.description: NIST released the initial public draft of SP 800-82 Revision 4, “Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security”, on 21 September, with comments open until 30 November 2026. The draft is reorganised around the Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, with the risk section refocused on the Govern function, and it expands the guidance on asset management, network monitoring and zero-trust architecture. Its coverage grows to building automation and control systems, water and wastewater, food and agriculture, freight rail, maritime vessels, and the convergence of industrial IoT with cloud services. Aviation is not among the sectors named. The building-automation material is the part that maps most directly onto an airport, because terminal HVAC, lighting, fire and access-control integration are building-automation systems, and they are often the least governed OT on the estate. This is draft guidance, not a requirement, and it places no new obligation on airports or airlines. - NIST Computer Security Resource Center publication page for the SP 800-82 Rev. 4 initial public draft; SecurityWeek coverage - Draft released 21 Sep 2026; comments due 30 Nov 2026

item.title: [Info] CISA’s Cyber Storm X ran a nation-state scenario against transportation, but the published scope names rail and ports, not aviation
item.category: Exercise — CISA national cyber exercise, transportation and water
item.description: CISA announced on 22 September that it had hosted Cyber Storm X, the latest in its national cyber exercise series. The four-day exercise brought together about 2,000 participants from more than 200 federal, state, local and private-sector organisations. The scenario was a nation-state adversary targeting the Transportation Systems sector, specifically rail and ports, and the Water and Wastewater Systems sector. Acting CISA Director Nick Andersen said the series “helps critical infrastructure owners and operators understand how we would manage a large-scale cyber incident.” CISA will produce a public after-action report of observations, analysis and recommendations. The published coverage gives no exact exercise dates. Aviation is not named in the scope. That is itself useful to know, because it means the national playbook tested this month was not rehearsed against an airport or airline scenario. The after-action report is still worth reading when it appears, because cross-sector coordination, information sharing and the federal-to-operator handoff are the same whichever mode of transport is attacked. - CISA news release on Cyber Storm X, reported by Industrial Cyber on 22 Sep 2026 (CISA page not reachable at generation time) - Announced 22 Sep 2026; public after-action report to follow

item.title: [Info] CISA publishes a cyber-decoys guide — the rare detection control you can add to an airport network without touching what it controls
item.category: Guidance — CISA, detection and response
item.description: CISA released “Using Cyber Decoys to Strengthen Detection and Response” on 17 September. The guide defines decoys as assets that look like legitimate systems, accounts or data but exist to distract an adversary, reveal their presence, or collect intelligence on how they operate, and it sets out three phases: preparation, execution and analysis. CISA positions the technique alongside Zero Trust rather than as a replacement for it. The reason it reads well for aviation is the constraint every airport security team knows: you cannot install an agent on a baggage controller, a jet-bridge PLC or an airfield-lighting panel, and a change window on those systems is expensive. A decoy is additive — a fake engineering workstation, a planted credential that no legitimate process should ever use, a file share named to look like integrator documentation — and it produces a signal with almost no false positives, because nothing legitimate should touch it. The catch is that a decoy nobody monitors is decoration, so the alerting path matters more than the decoy. - CISA guidance document — reporting via SecurityWeek and Industrial Cyber - Published 17 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] A US rule now counts a cyberattack as a “not controllable” cause of delay — and ties the relief to being compliant
item.category: Regulation & Policy — US Department of Transportation
item.description: A Department of Transportation rule reported on 11 September creates a new cause-of-delay category and designates ten types of disruption as “not controllable,” cyberattacks among them. Where a carrier is compliant with the cybersecurity regulations that apply to it, it no longer owes meals, hotels or comparable amenities under its customer service plan when one of those causes grounds flights; carriers that are not compliant remain subject to the requirements. Nothing here touches an aviation control system — this is advisory-only for OT. What it changes is the cost calculus behind a grounding cyber incident, and it puts a financial edge on being able to evidence compliance, because the carrier that can show it met its obligations is the one that keeps the relief. Reporting places the rule against the backdrop of the Scattered Spider intrusions at airlines, the Collins Aerospace incident that delayed European flights and the 2024 CrowdStrike outage, and notes there is no formal accounting of how often cyberattacks previously triggered compensation claims. Carried here factually as a regulatory change, with no comment on the policy debate around it. - US Department of Transportation rule — reporting via CyberScoop - Reported 11 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] ENISA switches on the Single Reporting Platform as the Cyber Resilience Act’s vulnerability reporting duties take effect
item.category: Regulation & Policy — EU Cyber Resilience Act
item.description: The EU Agency for Cybersecurity deployed the initial operating capability of its Single Reporting Platform, announced 14 September, giving manufacturers and open-source software stewards the channel they need to meet Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligations that took effect this month. Under the CRA, makers of products with digital elements must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents on a defined clock, with an early warning followed by a fuller notification. Airports and airlines are mostly beneficiaries here, but suppliers of baggage, BMS, access-control and airfield equipment placing products on the EU market now carry an active-exploitation reporting duty with a hard clock on it. Reported here factually as a regulatory milestone, without comment on the underlying policy debate. - ENISA announcement of the Single Reporting Platform initial operating capability — reporting via Industrial Cyber - Announced and reported 14 Sep 2026; CRA reporting obligations effective September 2026
